messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tunde is a 33-year-old African American man who has been struggling with symptoms following a traumatic event involving terrorism. Tunde works as a tailor and lives alone in an apartment near his shop in a bustling urban area. The trauma he experienced occurred about six months ago when a terrorist attack struck the city during a public festival. On that day, Tunde had gone to the festival after receiving a consignment of fabric for his tailoring business. The event was vibrant with music and dancing until an explosion shattered the atmosphere. In the chaos that followed, Tunde found himself caught in a panic-stricken crowd. He recalls bits and pieces but has memory gaps for critical moments during the attack. What he can remember is like a film playing over and over in his mind—images of people screaming, debris flying, and a pervasive sense of danger. Since then, Tunde’s life has been dramatically altered by his trauma. His tailoring shop, once a sanctuary filled with vibrant fabrics and patterns, now feels more like a place where he can hide from the world outside. He avoids going out as much as possible, spending long hours on his phone playing games or browsing the internet to avoid thinking about what happened. This habit has begun to affect his work; deadlines are slipping, and orders have been delayed because Tunde often loses track of time. When he does venture out, Tunde’s hypervigilance is palpable. He scans for exits as soon as he enters any room or building, ensuring that his back is always against a wall so he can see the entire space. This constant scanning and positioning leaves him feeling exhausted and on edge all the time. At times, he feels completely numb when recalling the event, as if it happened to someone else rather than himself. Tunde’s self-doubt has grown over time, exacerbated by his feelings of not belonging anywhere. He no longer trusts that he will do the right thing in a crisis and often wonders why he survived while others did not. This sense of weakness is overwhelming; he feels vulnerable and exposed, as if any moment could bring another attack. In an attempt to cope with these overwhelming emotions, Tunde sometimes seeks conflict or creates drama. He picks arguments with clients over minor issues, convinced that the attention will distract him from his trauma. These confrontations have strained relationships at work and led to several conflicts with suppliers, making it harder for him to maintain a stable business. Despite his efforts to avoid future plans, he has found himself increasingly isolated. Friends and family members have noticed his withdrawal and attempts to engage him in activities or outings are met with resistance. Tunde feels that planning anything might set him up for another disaster. This constant fear of what could happen next has made it difficult for him to connect with others on a meaningful level. It was the culmination of these issues—struggling at work, feeling isolated, and constantly living in fear—that finally brought Tunde to seek help. He is most afraid that he will never feel safe again, that every moment holds potential danger. Yet, there is also hope; he is hoping for some relief from his symptoms and a way to reclaim control over his life without feeling like he’s walking on eggshells all the time. Through therapy, Tunde hopes to regain trust in himself and find ways to engage with the world again without being constantly overwhelmed by fear. He wants to feel like he belongs somewhere and to reconnect with the sense of purpose he once had as a tailor, no longer overshadowed by his trauma.
